title: British jazz scene from 1949: Webb, Colyer, Littleton, Barber
summary: Stagg opens with the first British jazz bands he recalls, dance-band roots, George Webb's Dixielanders, Ken Colyer and Sonny Morris, Croydon concerts, Humphrey Lyttelton and the early Chris Barber band.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Tom Stagg of London, England, 3rd October 1969. Talking about jazz in England from the earliest recollection, I have is about 1949, at that time there were probably only two or three jazz bands, mainly based on the early dance bands of the period. The dance bands of that period were Billy Cotton and Harry Roy. The Savoy Havana Band and the Savoy Ophians, which played at the Savoy Hotel in London for a long period for many years, from the late 1920s, the British jazz bands originated from this type of music, probably partly due to the fact of the visit of the original Dixieland jazz band in 1919, where of course they used a British pianist, Billy Jones. Now the first recollection of a band I have, George Webb's Dixielanders, they played at a place called the Red Barn in Bexley Heath, Kent, which now is an outer London suburb, at that time was a separate Kent town. I can't recollect the personnel right now, but they played King Oliver numbers, and ODJB numbers, they were a very tightly arranged band, stuck mainly to the original scores and were pretty popular. They had, I can remember Bob D'Orban on trombone, who is now on the staff of the Melody Maker newspaper, writing on pop music, but at that time was a very good traditional style trombonist. This was the same time that Ken Collier became interested in, a little later, probably about 1950, 1951, Ken Collier came on the scene with a friend of his Sonny Morris. Sonny Morris still leads small bands of his own, but at that time the two played together in Middlesex, which again is now an outer London suburb, but at that time was a separate town. Now they played improvised jazz completely, there was much more earthy and ethnic folk music, they stuck nothing at all to any set arrangements or scores. They were playing, it's hard to say the tunes right now, they were playing tunes they'd heard on record, but not sticking to the, they were all 78s of King Oliver and Armstrong around at that time, they were sticking to these tunes, but they weren't sticking to the arrangements, they were just playing, this was the first improvised jazz in England. And they cut a few records for a small private label of their own, and then eventually on a label called, uh, A Squire, which was run by a fellow called Carlo Cramer, who is still active in England on the record producing side. The first jazz concerts I attended were probably around this time, about 1952, 53, after Ken Collier had left for New Orleans. The Mike Daniels band from Croydon, the Croydon area where I lived and always have lived, were around at that time, they were playing at the Croydon Jazz Club, a fellow by the name of Frank Getgood, who promoted in the Croydon area way back then, and still does today, he's one of the biggest promoters and enthusiasts in the South London area. And they used to, uh, to, uh, hold, uh, concerts at a place called the Civic Hall in Croydon, which is now pulled down, there's a, there's a big store in its place. And the Mike Daniels band used to play, the very early Humphrey Littleton band used to play there. And the Humphrey Littleton, the first Humphrey Littleton band I saw, uh, was made up of members of the Melody Maker, Paul Winners, award concert. At that time Eric Delaney, the drummer Eric Delaney, is now of course a showman, and a swing drummer, he's got his own little band, and he's on tour for, what, 52 weeks of the year, playing in holiday camps and ballrooms throughout the country. Humphrey Littleton at that time had, had a purely traditional style band of trumpet, trombone, clarinet, and drums, bass, and guitar he was using at that time. They were playing, uh, again, uh, mainly Armstrong and Oliver numbers, but Littleton must have been one of the first jazz musicians in England to write his own numbers and to arrange his own numbers, and these things are gradually, sort of, infiltrating into the British music scene. This is probably about 1953. Littleton also was one of the first, um, jazz bands to get a major recording contract with Parlophone records, and recorded extensively with Parlophone on 78s for, must have been ten years or so, probably as much as a, one issue a month at that time. And so he was the most well-known band at the time. The smaller bands around, the Ian Bell band, played at, uh, a place called the Park Lane Ballroom in Croydon, which was next door to the Fire Station. All been pulled down now. Uh, the Red River Jazz Band were around at that time. I can't remember the personnel. These were local bands. But mainly the Humphrey Littleton band at that time. There was also the Chris Barber band came into existence around that time. Uh, Collie was still away in New Orleans. Chris Barber had a small band of his own, mainly playing in the London area. They played at the Hammersmith's Palais for an Aspire record concert. Uh, Barber again was playing, he was playing sort of semi-arranged jazz even at that time, but putting in a few numbers of his own, probably following along the lines of the Humphrey Littleton band at that time.
